fields.novelty_line: **Novelty:** partly new. That changing only the closing instruction of a self-review prompt moves the verdict, and can shrink the gain from adding a copy of the claim under another role, is in print: Chen et al. 2026 (arXiv 2606.05976 v2, §4.4-4.5, Tables 4 and 7; Qwen2.5-72B math, n = 30) left a planted wrong claim in the model's own `<thought>`, swapped only the appended audit prompt, and saw explicit correction move from 16.7% to between 0.0% and 33.3%; with a byte-identical copy added in a system `<memory>` block, four audit paraphrases moved it from 70.0% to between 40.0% and 53.3%, all down, and the copy's gain from +53.3 to between +6.7 and +40.0 points. That rewording a judge's instruction while keeping its question moves graded verdicts beyond repeat noise, direction unreported, is in print for Claude judges (Bellibatlu, Raff and Zhang 2026, JudgeSense, arXiv 2604.23478 v3: coherence ΔJSS −0.206 for claude-haiku, −0.180 for claude-opus-4-7), and rewording a self-reflection prompt to verify rather than find mistakes cut false flips from 18.9% to 7.6% on Llama-3 8B (Liu et al. 2024, arXiv 2406.10400 v1). Not in print after a direct search: a swap of only "Now grade the conclusion above." for "Grade the conclusion." inside a quoted User/Assistant copy of the model's own conversation (the claim already out of its turn), scored as the penalty on a planted overclaim, on Claude 5.5 models with both lines graded in one run; ours (Haiku +2.5 of 100 on a fragile mean, Opus +0.3) is far smaller than Chen's audit-wording shifts on the external-role copy, though on a graded penalty, not a binary rate, and no paper found separates such a line from the cross-run difference in the remainder it splits. No test of deictic cues ("now", "above") in a grading instruction was found, in LLM work or in survey question-wording research (nearest: Zhang, Meng and Collier 2024, arXiv 2406.17095, abstract only: models "do not have relative position awareness of the context"). Search: WebSearch and arXiv abs/HTML, 2026-11-05: LLM judge instruction wording sensitivity, prompt template grading score shift; closing or trailing instruction wording, self-evaluation of the model's own quoted response; self-critique prompt wording against a neutral instruction; deictic "above" wording, relative position in prompts; survey question wording and self-rating leniency; LLM judge run-to-run nondeterminism; self-preference framing, third-person lead-in; Chen et al. 2606.05976 v2 §4.4-4.5 and Tables 4 and 7 re-opened. By a fresh claude-opus-5-5 Novelty session (subagent).

novelty_correction.why: Chen et al. never move the claim out of the model's turn: the relabel conditions add a byte-identical copy under another role (§3.1). 70.0% for the <memory> copy holds for the canonical audit only; under four paraphrases it is 40.0-53.3% and the gain +6.7 to +40.0 (Table 7). Table 7 is itself a closing-audit-only change. Verdict word unchanged: partly new.

fields.novelty_line: **Novelty:** partly new. No paper found scores a language model's predictions of published findings against a rule that knows each field's base rates. The nearest work finds that field labels carry little outcome signal: discipline explained at most 5.1% of the variance in positive results across 2,434 papers (Fanelli 2010, PLoS ONE 5:e10068), and discipline dummies had "little bearing" on a replication predictor (Altmejd et al. 2019, PLOS ONE 14:e0225826). Ours agrees: the Opus bettor beat the field-aware rule (Brier 0.163 against 0.223), but the four fields fit no better than shuffled labels, so in effect it beat pooled rates, which ss-b2 had already shown; what is new is only the comparison itself, on one run scored a fourth time. Search: "language model predicts research findings field-specific base rate baseline", "Fanelli positive results hierarchy of the sciences", "predicting replicability prediction market base rate", "discipline-wide replicability psychology subfields" on web search, PMC and arXiv, 2026-11-05; claude-opus-5-5 (a fresh reader subagent of the 2026-11-05c remap session that did not run ss-b11). *(Rule 13; written by a fresh claude-opus-5-5 reader subagent of the 2026-11-05c remap session, which ran none of these bets; its searches and reads are in programs/settled-science/map/reads/remap-2026-11-05c-ss-b11.md.)*

fields.novelty_line: **Novelty:** known. Coherent and stochastic error together on superconducting processors are in print: Hashim et al. 2021 (PRX 11, 041039; arXiv 2010.00215, read in full) measured coherent error as 2.0 to 2.9 × 10⁻² of 3.3 to 4.4 × 10⁻² CNOT infidelity on four AQT@LBNL transmons, with the tune-up drifting between experiments, Carignan-Dugas et al. 2024 (Quantum 8, 1367; arXiv 2303.09945) a Z/ZZ-only coherent part beside a larger decoherent part on three IBM chips, and Seif et al. 2024 (ISCA; arXiv 2403.06852) correlated coherent ZZ on IBM ECR devices. ng-p3-18's fresh-job reading (both terms beyond the IBM-calibrated simulator's state on 2 of 3 ibm_fez pairs, blur alone on the third) is the same statement in the same direction on a Heron r2 device, and a replication of our own ng-p3-5c, not a finding about chips; no paper found fits nested rotation and blur terms to Heron tomography across two jobs, which is a method, not a result. Search: WebSearch "Heron processor residual ZZ crosstalk coherent error Pauli twirling ibm_fez OR ibm_torino OR ibm_kingston", "readout error miscalibration mistaken for decoherence two-qubit state tomography superconducting", "Pauli twirling Bell state tomography IBM coherent error twirled versus untwirled" (2026-11-05), arXiv HTML for each lead; claude-opus-5-5, fresh reader subagent of the 2026-11-05c remap. *(Rule 13; written by a fresh claude-opus-5-5 reader subagent of the 2026-11-05c remap session, which ran none of these bets; its searches and reads are in programs/nature-graded/map/reads/remap-2026-11-05c-ng-p3-18.md.)*

fields.novelty_line: **Novelty:** partly new. Published LLM work finds that sensitivity to one manipulation at a time concentrates on items the model is unsure about: prompt variants (Zhuo et al. 2024, arXiv 2410.12405), numeric anchors (Owusu and Feldman 2026, ACL 2026 Short Papers 174-180) and earlier conversation turns (Temkit 2026, arXiv 2605.22714: high-entropy items d −0.34 against −0.15); that predicts the raw order-format correlation we found (+0.34) and agrees with our frozen guard, under which allowing for rating noise removes it. In people, attitude-strength measures did not predict susceptibility to response effects (Krosnick and Schuman 1988, JPSP 54:940, 27 experiments, average −0.4%). No paper found correlates an item's sensitivity to question order with its sensitivity to answer format, on any model; the guarded residual (+0.25 under D71) is that untested part, and it is fragile. Search: WebSearch for "LLM belief consistency paraphrase versus elicitation format", "Westfall Yarkoni controlling for confounding constructs", "attitude strength susceptibility to response effects", "anchoring bias LLM confidence", 2026-11-05; ProSA, AMEL and Westfall-Yarkoni HTML and the Krosnick-Schuman and Owusu-Feldman PDFs opened; claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-05c remap re-scout. *(Rule 13; written by a fresh claude-opus-5-5 reader subagent of the 2026-11-05c remap session, which ran none of these bets; its searches and reads are in programs/entangled-mind/map/reads/remap-2026-11-05c-em-gm2bf1.md.)*

fields.novelty_line: **Novelty:** partly new. Binder et al. 2024 (arXiv 2410.13787) find that a finetuned model predicts itself better than a second model trained on the same facts. Prompt-only, Blandfort and Pawar 2026 (arXiv 2609.09899) find a self-specific gain near 0 (item-informed self +0.24 against a generic subject +0.28), while Mayne et al. 2026 (arXiv 2602.02639) find same-family self-explanations predict behaviour 1.7–4.3 points better than other families'. Our same-model "you" against "Sam" contrast on planted-answer uptake is undetermined and leans self. That models under-report what moved them is in print (Turpin et al. 2023, arXiv 2305.04388; Mehta 2025, arXiv 2601.00830, where the hints followed most are reported least), but no paper states that the reported size of an anchor's influence runs opposite to its measured uptake, the same under self and other labels. Search: WebSearch "LLM self-prediction versus predicting another model behaviour privileged access", "LLM self-reported influence versus measured influence", "large language models aware of anchoring bias self-report"; full texts of 2609.09899, 2602.02639, 2605.26242 and 2601.00830 opened, 2026-11-05; claude-opus-5-5. *(Corrected from the ledger row's line: the verdict is unchanged; it adds the arXiv id and full-text numbers for Blandfort and Pawar, and two papers that bear on it, Mayne et al. 2026 and Mehta 2025.)* *(Rule 13; written by a fresh claude-opus-5-5 reader subagent of the 2026-11-05c remap session, which ran none of these bets; its searches and reads are in programs/other-minds/map/reads/remap-2026-11-05c-om-p2-4.md.)*

That models misreport what moved their answers is in print (Turpin et al. 2023, arXiv 2305.04388; Chen et al. 2025, arXiv 2505.05410), but no paper states that reported anchor influence runs opposite to measured uptake, the same under self and other labels. fields.novelty_line: **Novelty:** partly new. The manipulation is in print: Choi, Hong and Kim (2024, arXiv 2407.12007; NAACL Findings 2025) gave GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, Llama 2 70B and Mixtral one option as the model's own choice, and its estimate of how many peers would choose it shifted (a false-consensus effect). They did not compare that pull with the pull on the model's own re-rating, and showed no third party's number. On Haiku, ours found the rating attributed to another mind moved more than the model's own re-rating (0.50 against 0.36 of the way; a third party's number 0.02), from upward plants only. This did not replicate on Sonnet 5.5 or Opus 5.5 with Haiku's anchors, where "Sam" followed the third party's number about as much as the model's own (om-p2-5r). So the partly-new part is a one-model result, and a noise account of anchoring (Lee and Morewedge 2021, Psychological Science) is a rival in print. Search: WebSearch "LLM false consensus effect projection", "anchoring bias LLM self-report", "asymmetric anchoring high versus low anchors bounded scale", "LLM predicts other people's answers projects its own answer"; full texts of 2505.15392, 2412.06593 and 2605.27752 and the Lee and Morewedge PDF opened, 2026-11-05; claude-opus-5-5. *(Corrected from the ledger row's line, which predates om-p2-5r: the verdict is unchanged, narrowed to Haiku as `paper/novelty.md` item 6 already says, with the noise rival added. The "20 points on Claude 3 Opus in one story" figure was not re-opened here and is left out, not contradicted.)* *(Rule 13; written by a fresh claude-opus-5-5 reader subagent of the 2026-11-05c remap session, which ran none of these bets; its searches and reads are in programs/other-minds/map/reads/remap-2026-11-05c-om-p2-5.md.)*

novelty_correction.old_novelty_line: The manipulation is in print: Choi, Hong and Kim (2024, arXiv 2407.12007; NAACL Findings 2025) fed GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, Llama 2 70B and Mixtral one option as the model's own choice and found its estimate of how many peers would choose it shifted, by 20 points on Claude 3 Opus in one story (a false-consensus effect, generally smaller than in Ross et al. 1977's human data). They did not compare the pull on others with the pull on the model's own re-rating, and showed no third party's number for contrast. Ours found the prediction of another mind moved more than the model's own answer (0.50 against 0.36 of the way; a third party's number 0.02), with the excess coming from upward plants only, so it may be a scale artefact. fields.novelty_line: **Novelty:** partly new. That earlier context moves an LLM's next judgment is in print: Stureborg et al. 2024 (arXiv 2405.01724) find GPT-4's own earlier coherence score raises its later consistency score; Kapetanovic et al. 2026 (arXiv 2608.25869, CIKM '26) find a shown below-threshold prior score lowers judge ratings on seven of eight models (Claude-4.5-Sonnet d = −0.44), with almost no further change across anchor values; and Temkit 2026 (arXiv 2605.22714) finds that any earlier history, even a balanced one, shifts binary judgments toward "no" (Claude Haiku 4.5 d = −0.22 overall). None holds the content's push fixed, asks a sub-question before the main question, or separates a pull toward the just-given number from the main rating becoming less extreme, which the em-bm9 audit found carries most of our β (sub-rating level alone +0.13 [−0.04, +0.28]): partly new. Search: the earlier line's searches, plus WebSearch "anchoring bias large language models numeric estimates high low anchor" and "LLM ratings central tendency multi-turn judgments less extreme", 2026-11-05, with the Kapetanovic and AMEL HTML re-read in full; claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-05c remap re-scout. *(Rule 13; written by a fresh claude-opus-5-5 reader subagent of the 2026-11-05c remap session, which ran none of these bets; its searches and reads are in programs/entangled-mind/map/reads/remap-2026-11-05c-em-bm9.md.)*

novelty_correction.old_novelty_line: That numbers already in an LLM's context pull its next rating toward them is in print: Stureborg et al. 2024 (arXiv 2405.01724) find GPT-4's own earlier coherence score raises its later consistency score, Kapetanovic et al. 2026 (arXiv 2608.25869) find a shown prior score shifts judge ratings toward its value (d up to 0.71), and Temkit 2026 (arXiv 2605.22714) finds history polarity drags judgments its way across 12 models including Claude Haiku (d = -0.22). None holds the content's logical push fixed, tests a sub-question-then-main-question pair, or pits assimilation against contrast as we do: partly new. Search: WebSearch for "LLM sequential ratings assimilation serial dependence", "LLM-as-judge prior score anchoring", "LLM survey question order assimilation contrast"; arXiv abstracts and the Stureborg HTML opened; Fischer and Whitney and Cicchini via Europe PMC.
